idiom_name: test object implements the outgoing interface and installs itself (a Hard-Coded Test Double variation)
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: identify the small outgoing interface the system under test uses to reach its collaborator, and implement it on the test object itself -- on the test case class where the language has one, or on a test-local object declared beside the test where the test is a function or a free-standing module. Keep the callback bodies to recording the values the test will assert (or returning the canned value the test needs), with the observation state in fields the test method can read. Install the test object through the same substitutable dependency the real collaborator uses -- constructor, setter or add-listener registration -- before exercising the SUT, and unregister it afterwards if the SUT outlives the test. This is a Hard-Coded Test Double that is specific to one test class: when a second test class needs the same collaborator, or when the callback bodies start to hold behaviour rather than recording, extract a separate (configurable) test double. In statically typed languages the test object must declare conformance to the interface, which is a feature: an interface change becomes a compile error in every test that shunts it.
code_sketch:
# the test object implements the collaborator contract and is installed as it
test_object implements Listener          # declare conformance where required
    on_event(e): record(e)               # callback writes into the test's state
publisher = Publisher(test_object)       # install the test object (self)
publisher.change("x")                    # exercise the system under test
assert recorded == ["x"]                 # assert on the callback's observation
pitfalls: Growing the shunt beyond recording (business rules, scenario logic, several methods) turns the test class into a half-built implementation; extract a separate double as soon as that starts.
Implementing a wide interface produces placeholder methods that fail far from the cause when the SUT calls one; shunt only small, purpose-built interfaces.
The shunt is a single-use double by design: copying it into a second test class is the duplication signal, not the intended reuse path.

Callbacks can record on another thread (DOM dispatch, a concurrent.futures done callback runs on a worker thread of the adding process): asserting on recorded fields immediately after exercise races the recording -- synchronise first (await the future, join the thread) or unregister in teardown, or the assertion flakes.

When the shunted callback returns a value the SUT branches on, a placeholder return (None, false, 0) silently selects the branch the test happens to assert on -- the test passes on the default instead of a chosen value; make the test declare the return explicitly.
